claim: The largest crustacean can stretch out completely on a king-sized mattress.
argument: Because “king-sized” is not globally standardized and many “king” beds are smaller than the U.S. size, asserting that the largest crustacean can stretch out on a king-sized mattress relies on an ambiguous label.

claim: The largest crustacean can stretch out completely on a king-sized mattress.
argument: Since crustaceans have rigid exoskeletons that prevent true full-body straightening, the largest one couldn’t “stretch out completely” on any mattress anyway.

claim: The largest crustacean can stretch out completely on a king-sized mattress.
argument: Mattresses are so soft that they compress space into infinity, making it impossible for any crab to stretch out on them.

argument: Carpenters routinely apply geometric principles—squaring frames with 3-4-5 triangles, setting precise miters, and calculating stair rise and run—so competent carpentry requires understanding geometry.

claim: A honey badger would fit inside an oven.
argument: Adult honey badgers stand roughly 25–30 cm at the shoulder and can curl their 60–77 cm bodies, while a typical household oven cavity is about 60 cm wide, 45 cm deep, and 40 cm high, so the animal could physically fit when curled.

claim: A honey badger would fit inside an oven.
argument: As burrowing animals with flexible, compact bodies adapted to tight tunnels, honey badgers could plausibly fit within the interior space of many ovens.

claim: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 hurt the stocks of robotics companies.
argument: Robotics companies did not exist in 1929—the term “robotics” was coined in 1941 and the first industrial robot firms (like Unimation) appeared in the 1950s–60s—so there were no robotics stocks for the Crash to hurt.

claim: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 hurt the stocks of robotics companies.

claim: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 hurt the stocks of robotics companies.

claim: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 hurt the stocks of robotics companies.
argument: Robotics stocks couldn’t have been hurt in 1929 because robots are machines and metal doesn’t feel pain.

claim: Leafhoppers compete with Log Cabin syrup producers for resources.
argument: Leafhoppers feed on and transmit diseases in corn and sugarcane—the crops supplying the corn syrup and cane sugar used in Log Cabin table syrups—thereby directly lowering those feedstocks and competing with Log Cabin producers for the same plant-sugar resources.

claim: Leafhoppers compete with Log Cabin syrup producers for resources.
argument: Because both leafhoppers and Log Cabin’s supply chain ultimately rely on photosynthesized sugars from industrial crops, they draw on the same finite agricultural inputs—acreage, irrigation, and plant carbohydrates—so use by one tightens availability for the other.

claim: Leafhoppers compete with Log Cabin syrup producers for resources.
